I joined the DeMON Lab in 2025 as a postdoc researcher, after completing a PhD in the Neuropresage Team (Caen, France). My scientific curiosity has long revolved around the hippocampus and its resilience mechanisms, which led me to explore medial temporal lobe alterations in aging and Alzheimer’s disease through neuroimaging — falling for fMRI along the way.
I traded my French seahorse for the Swedish archipelago — hoping to squeeze in some backpacking adventures across the northern landscapes. At the lab, I continue to tackle fundamental questions about Alzheimer’s disease pathophysiology. My current focus is to elucidate how the dynamics between brain network activity and toxic protein accumulation orchestrate the pathological cascade of Alzheimer’s disease.

Jake is the head of the DeMON Lab and the director of the Neurodegenerative Research Unit at the Department of Clinical Science Malmö at Lund University. As a SciLifeLab and Wallenberg National Program Data-driven Life Sciences (DDLS) fellow, Jake is a proud member of SciLifeLab, and is also a member of Multi-Park Lund. Jake trained at UC-Berkeley, got his PhD at McGill University, and did a postdoc at the University of Pennsylvania, becoming an expert along the way in neuroimaging, aging, AI and bioinformatics. He now dedicates his time toward better understanding how neurodegenerative diseases work, and building innovative tools to improve clinical care.
Outside the lab, Jake is an active musician, an avid (indoor) boulderer, an inveterate beer snob, a frequent traveler, and a die-hard fan of the Philadelphia Eagles. He’s also been known to consort with the queen.

Jonathan is a PhD student studying how brain connectivity changes across aging and Alzheimer’s disease. With a background in statistics and cognitive science, his work focuses on large-scale neuroimaging datasets to better understand how functional brain networks reorganize in the face of pathology.
On his free time Jonathan enjoys building and tinkering – whether it’s constructing a tiny self-sufficient house, developing new brain visualization tools, or building various applications. If a problem exists he likes trying to solve it (though he admits he often creates new ones in the process).

Sophie joined the DeMON Lab in 2026 as an assistant researcher. Her PhD at the Amsterdam UMC and Lund University focused on heterogeneity in neurodegenerative diseases. Her main interests are disease progression modeling to estimate the timing, sequence, and regional distribution of pathological changes and variability therein, and the effects of co-pathologies on clinical progression.

Ruoyi graduated with a Master’s degree in Machine Learning from Lund University in September 2024 and joined the lab immediately after. She is currently focusing on developing deep learning methods for the automated segmentation of medial temporal lobe (MTL) subregions in histological data to advance the understanding of neurodegenerative pathology. Driven by academic curiosity, she is interested in exploring how AI models can reveal the hidden structural patterns in either images or clinical data that may provide new insights into the progression of neurodegenerative disease.
Outside of research, Ruoyi enjoys hiking and exploring nature, having trekked Kungsleden, Trolltunga, and Stoos, with her next goal being the Camino de Santiago. She also takes time to recharge through camping, skiing, and watching movies.

title: DeMON
text:
About the Lab
In the DeMON Lab, we investigate how neurodegenerative diseases develop and progress over time. Our research focuses primarily on Alzheimer’s disease but also other neurodegenerative disorders, with the goal of identifying biological changes at any stage of the disease, even those that precede clinical symptoms, and understanding why individuals experience disease differently.
To address these questions, we integrate large-scale neuroimaging, molecular, genetic, and clinical datasets. By combining statistical learning, disease progression modelling, and multi-omics approaches, we develop computational methods that model disease progression, reveal patterns of heterogeneity in these diseases, identify biologically meaningful subtypes, and improve our understanding of disease mechanisms.
Our research group is also privileged with a large network of collaborators that help push forward the lab’s research goals by providing both expert domain knowledge and rare datasets.
We are committed to open and reproducible science, FAIR data principles, and the development of methods and resources that benefit the wider research community.

Latest from the Lab








Figure from this paper (CC BY-NC 4.0).
Latest publication
Romina Zendehdel et al., bioRxiv, Nov 10, 2026
Beyond organ age gaps: comparing plasma proteomic metrics of organ biology in relation to brain structure and neurodegenerative disease
Neurodegenerative diseases mainly affect the brain, but biological changes throughout the body may matter too. Using plasma proteomics from over 50,000 UK Biobank participants, we compared three organ-level proteomic metrics (organ age gap, PC1 and PLS1) in relation to brain structure and disease risk. Aging of specific organs was linked to thinning of specific brain regions. Organ age gaps predicted incident neurological disease best of the three, but added only modestly to prediction models.

title: Research
text:
We combine brain imaging, molecular data and computational modelling to understand how
neurodegenerative diseases begin, spread and differ between people. Our work falls into four
connected themes: PET, fMRI, omics and AI.









PET

tau subtypes & spread







fMRI

brain networks







Omics

proteomics & single-cell







AI

machine learning







Software

open tools









PET
tau subtypes & spread



Alzheimer's disease does not unfold the same way in everyone. Using tau-PET imaging and disease progression modelling, we discovered that tau spreads through the brain along four distinct trajectories: limbic, MTL-sparing, posterior and lateral temporal.
Tau does not appear everywhere at once: it travels along the brain's connections. By modelling this spread on brain networks we can explain where tau appears, and we now build personalised models that forecast how each person's disease may evolve.
















Four tau subtypes















Figures adapted from this paper.








Four distinct trajectories of tau deposition identified in Alzheimer's disease

Jacob Vogel et al. 
· 
Nature Medicine
 · 
Apr 29, 2021





Using tau-PET scans from 1,612 individuals, we identified four distinct trajectories of tau pathology: limbic, MTL-sparing, posterior and lateral temporal. These subtypes were stable over follow-up, replicated in a separate sample with a different radiotracer, and showed distinct demographic and cognitive profiles and outcomes, suggesting a re-examination of the idea of 'typical' Alzheimer's disease.

Read the paper













fMRI
brain networks



Brain communication is organised along several axes that shape how resources are distributed from moment to moment, and may underlie key cognitive processes. Using a whole-brain framework, we found that ageing reshapes communication along one of these axes, while Alzheimer's disease affects an entirely different one.













Age and AD along separate axes














Figures from this paper.








Different functional connectivity gradients reflect aging and Alzheimer's disease

Jonathan Rittmo et al. 
· 
Nature Neuroscience
 · 
Oct 1, 2026





In two independent cohorts (BioFINDER-2, N = 973; ADNI, N = 129), functional connectivity changes linked to aging and to Alzheimer's disease aligned with separate axes of brain communication. Early AD pathology and later cognitive decline followed the sensory-association axis, while age-related change followed the representation-executive axis across the adult lifespan.

Read the paper













Omics
proteomics & single-cell



Every cell type in the brain responds to Alzheimer's disease in its own way. Using single-nucleus RNA sequencing, we found a coordinated, multi-cellular response to AD pathology in one dataset and replicated it cleanly in a completely independent one: a reference point for future perturbation and drug-development studies.
We bring the same care for robustness to proteins: spinal-fluid reference proteins make biomarkers more accurate and easier to interpret.
















Analysis workflow















Figures from this paper (CC BY-NC 4.0).








A coordinated and reproducible multicellular response to AD pathology

Gabriele Vilkaite et al. 
· 
bioRxiv
 · 
Oct 23, 2026





Single-cell studies of the Alzheimer's brain often report differing results and rarely consider how cell types respond together. Across 2.3 million nuclei from 427 ROSMAP donors, we identified multicellular signatures of AD pathology and of sex, including profound changes in RORB-GABRG excitatory neurons and disrupted oligodendrocyte precursor signalling. These signatures predicted neuropathology and sex in a fully independent dataset (SEA-AD), giving a baseline against which perturbation and treatment experiments can be compared.

Read the paper













AI
machine learning



We use machine learning and deep learning to diagnose dementias from proteins, and to predict or even generate tau-PET scans from cheaper, more widely available data such as MRI and blood tests.
We also hold these models to a high standard: we have shown how data leakage makes models look better while they actually generalise worse, and built tools to prevent it.
















Model workflow















Figures adapted from this paper (CC BY 4.0).








A deep joint-learning proteomics model for diagnosis of six conditions associated with dementia

Lijun An et al. 
· 
Nature Medicine
 · 
Mar 31, 2026





Mixed pathologies make dementia hard to diagnose, and scalable biomarkers are missing for most of them. We present ProtAIDe-Dx, a deep joint-learning model trained on 17,187 patients and controls that uses plasma proteomics to diagnose six conditions at once, with a balanced accuracy of 70-95%. It improved differential diagnosis in a memory clinic sample and shows which proteins drive each person's result, all from a single blood draw.

Read the paper













Software

A Python package that checks machine-learning pipelines for data leakage. It uses label permutation to test whether a pipeline performs above chance when no true signal is present.

Plumber
A web tool for checking data leakage using large language models. Paste a method section, select the leakage checks, and it builds a structured review prompt to copy into an LLM.

Lijun grew up in China and earned his Ph.D. in Electrical and Computer Engineering from the National University of Singapore. He later joined Lund University, where he is currently a postdoctoral researcher in the DeMON Lab..
His research focuses on developing machine learning algorithms for multi-modal data (e.g., brain imaging and multi-omics) to advance our understanding of neurodegenerative diseases. Lijun believes that future scientific breakthroughs will be driven by algorithms that can uncover new insights from massive data across scientific disciplines. Currently, he is working on several exciting projects together with his talented lab colleagues. To learn more, visit his homepage: https://anlijun.cn.
Outside the lab, Lijun enjoys hiking and writing humorous Chinese poetry.

Rosa is a data scientist and statistician with a PhD in Mathematical Statistics and more than nine years of experience in data science research for bioinformatics. She is an assistant researcher in the DeMON Lab at Lund University.
Her research has covered gene regulatory networks, Bayesian networks, hidden Markov models and statistical modelling, with applications in cancer genomics, drug repurposing for COVID-19, and microbiome studies of the gut, lakes and soil. In the DeMON Lab, she is now working on identifying tau subtypes in Alzheimer’s disease.
Outside the lab, Rosa loves spending time with her daughter, being in the mountains, and meeting people and hearing about their cultures. She enjoys cooking and trying new food, watching American TV series, and reading books and poetry in her native Persian. She also follows the news, perhaps a little too closely.

Romina Zendehdel et al.
bioRxiv
Nov 10, 2026






Beyond organ age gaps: comparing plasma proteomic metrics of organ biology in relation to brain structure and neurodegenerative disease

Neurodegenerative diseases mainly affect the brain, but biological changes throughout the body may matter too. Using plasma proteomics from over 50,000 UK Biobank participants, we compared three organ-level proteomic metrics (organ age gap, PC1 and PLS1) in relation to brain structure and disease risk. Aging of specific organs was linked to thinning of specific brain regions. Organ age gaps predicted incident neurological disease best of the three, but added only modestly to prediction models.

Gabriele Vilkaite et al.
bioRxiv
Oct 23, 2026






A coordinated and reproducible multicellular response to AD pathology

Single-cell studies of the Alzheimer's brain often report differing results and rarely consider how cell types respond together. Across 2.3 million nuclei from 427 ROSMAP donors, we identified multicellular signatures of AD pathology and of sex, including profound changes in RORB-GABRG excitatory neurons and disrupted oligodendrocyte precursor signalling. These signatures predicted neuropathology and sex in a fully independent dataset (SEA-AD), giving a baseline against which perturbation and treatment experiments can be compared.

Jonathan Rittmo et al.
Nature Neuroscience
Oct 1, 2026






Different functional connectivity gradients reflect aging and Alzheimer's disease

In two independent cohorts (BioFINDER-2, N = 973; ADNI, N = 129), functional connectivity changes linked to aging and to Alzheimer's disease aligned with separate axes of brain communication. Early AD pathology and later cognitive decline followed the sensory-association axis, while age-related change followed the representation-executive axis across the adult lifespan.

Lijun An et al.
Nature Medicine
Mar 31, 2026






A deep joint-learning proteomics model for diagnosis of six conditions associated with dementia

Mixed pathologies make dementia hard to diagnose, and scalable biomarkers are missing for most of them. We present ProtAIDe-Dx, a deep joint-learning model trained on 17,187 patients and controls that uses plasma proteomics to diagnose six conditions at once, with a balanced accuracy of 70-95%. It improved differential diagnosis in a memory clinic sample and shows which proteins drive each person's result, all from a single blood draw.

Jacob Vogel et al.
Nature Medicine
Apr 29, 2021






Four distinct trajectories of tau deposition identified in Alzheimer's disease

Using tau-PET scans from 1,612 individuals, we identified four distinct trajectories of tau pathology: limbic, MTL-sparing, posterior and lateral temporal. These subtypes were stable over follow-up, replicated in a separate sample with a different radiotracer, and showed distinct demographic and cognitive profiles and outcomes, suggesting a re-examination of the idea of 'typical' Alzheimer's disease.

Jacob Vogel et al.
Nature Communications
May 26, 2020






Spread of pathological tau proteins through communicating neurons in human Alzheimer's disease

Animal models suggest that tau spreads from cell to cell through neuronal connections. We tested this in 312 people along the Alzheimer's continuum using an epidemic spreading model, which explained up to 70% of the variance in the spatial pattern of tau. Our results provide evidence in humans that tau spreads through neuronal communication pathways, and that beta-amyloid accelerates this process.
